game_side.target: Which team wins (regulation or including OT/SO per the contract wording), by margin or puck-line spread where applicable.
game_side.mechanism: Win probability is driven by the difference in team goal-scoring and goal-prevention quality (xG-based, goalie-adjusted), shifted by home ice, rest and lineup/goalie news, and then mapped onto a settlement rule: including overtime and shootout the outcome is nearly 50/50 conditional on a regulation tie, while regulation-only and margin contracts depend on the goal-difference distribution.

inputs.why: Team offensive process is the core of win probability once adjusted for opponent and score effects.
Team defensive process determines opponent shot quality; must be lineup-adjusted for the specific game.
Starter identity moves expected goals against by tenths per game and is the largest same-day information event.
Shrunk GSAx converts a given shot-quality environment into goals against.
Absences of top skaters change both rating and special teams; timing of news matters.
PP/PK matchup alters goals expected, scaled by penalty-rate expectations.
Rest and back-to-back status affect skaters and shift goalie starts to backups.
Home ice advantage is modest but persistent; some rinks also alter measured shot counts.
Short-run goals and record carry shooting and save luck that should be regressed.
Overtime and shootout rules decide the tail of tied regulation games in including-OT contracts.
A calibrated rating prior stabilises game-level estimates.
Market price and its moves after goalie/lineup news are the benchmark to beat.
Whether OT/SO counts defines the contract.
De-vigged sharp lines are a strong competing probability estimate.
Home last change steers matchups and slightly boosts the home team beyond generic home ice.
Replacement-level depth quality when regulars are out changes the lineup-adjusted team rating.
Spread and depth decide whether a modelled edge survives execution costs.
Price-dependent fees set the breakeven probability for the edge.
Trade flow around goalie confirmation shows speed and direction of information incorporation.
Settlement values calibrate the model and expose OT/SO and correction edge cases.

interactions.hypothesis: Goalie quality matters most against high-danger-shot teams: the effect of a starter switch should be modelled as GSAx times the opponent's expected shot-danger volume, not a constant.
Back-to-back fatigue interacts with starter rotation: the net effect of a back-to-back is mostly the backup goalie, so the flag should be conditioned on confirmed starter.
Regression of PDO should be partial: teams whose xG-implied finishing and goalie talent justify higher SH%/SV% should regress less.

game_total.target: Total goals (or one team's goals) in regulation or the full game as defined by the contract, including empty-net goals; and both-teams-to-score style thresholds.
game_total.mechanism: Goals are a function of shot volume, shot quality, goalie conversion and special-teams time for each team; totals are the sum of two overdispersed count processes with a small positive correlation through pace and empty-net goals. Inputs that change the number or quality of chances (pace, xG, goalies, penalty expectation) shift the mean, while script and EN dynamics shape the tail.

inputs.why: Combined shot-attempt volume sets the number of chances available.
Quality of chances each team creates scales total expected goals.
Opponent suppression quality caps or expands scoring.
Starting goalie quality changes goals against by large amounts game to game.
Convert shot quality to goals; needs shrinkage.
Expected power-play minutes add high-yield scoring time.
PP/PK efficiency converts penalty minutes into goals.
EN goals add to totals when games are close late.
Crew tendencies change penalties called, shifting PP opportunities.
Tired teams and backup goalies raise scoring.
Tail rungs price dispersion not just the mean.
Rink scoring environment and shot counting bias.
Threshold rungs reveal market's implied distribution.
Whether OT, SO goal, EN goal count for totals.
Trade flow after goalie confirmation indicates how the market re-priced totals.
Thin depth on total rungs affects executable edge.

interactions.hypothesis: Pace and goalie quality combine multiplicatively: high-event games with weak goalies produce fat right tails, high-event games with strong goalies mostly add saves not goals.
Penalty expectation is the product of team taken/drawn rates, crew tendency and PP efficiency; each alone overstates the effect.
EN goals are concentrated in games decided by one goal late; interacting spread with coach pull timing gives their expected contribution to the total.

game_event.target: Whether the game reaches overtime, a shootout or multiple overtimes (playoffs), under the contract's exact definition.
game_event.mechanism: Overtime requires a regulation tie, whose probability is a function of the goal-difference distribution (low totals and close spreads raise it); shootout requires the tie to survive a 3v3 overtime in the regular season, and multi-overtime events apply to playoff games where 20-minute sudden-death periods continue until a goal. Base rates by season type and totals dominate, with team style and goalie quality shifting the tail.

inputs.why: Directly gives P(tie after 60), the base of every OT market.
Lower totals and tighter dispersion raise tie frequency.
Closeness of the pregame spread controls tie probability.
Controls how often 3v3 resolves before a shootout.
Shrunk shootout talent for shootout win markets.
Strong goalies reduce goals and raise tie probability.
Playoff vs regular season changes OT format and shootout existence.
Late pulls convert one-goal deficits into ties or empty-net goals.
Wording defines regulation tie, OT and shootout and multi-OT counts.
Market price baseline for event contracts.

interactions.hypothesis: Low-total, low-spread games raise tie probability, so the interaction of total goals expectation and spread should drive P(tie) rather than either alone.
Shootout probability = P(tie) x P(3v3 not decisive); team 3v3 scoring and goalie quality in OT jointly determine the second factor.
In playoffs the shootout does not exist and multi-OT events depend on 5v5 sudden-death scoring rates, so the playoff flag changes the model structure not just parameters.

period.target: Winner, goal total, spread or both-teams-score within a single period (1st, 2nd or 3rd).
period.mechanism: Period outcomes are small-sample versions of the full-game process with period-specific shapes: first periods are cagier, second periods have long changes, third periods are dominated by score effects and empty-net goals. With ties common (period winner can tie), the distribution is heavily discrete and sensitive to the goalie and the first-minutes deployment.

inputs.why: Period-specific scoring and shot shape for each team.
Chance quality creation per 20 minutes.
Chance suppression per 20 minutes.
Goalie identity drives period goals against; warm-up matters in period one.
Third-period behaviour depends on lead/trail state.
PP chances concentrate in particular periods.
Line deployment per period (top lines early).
Second-period change dynamics.
Late third-period EN goals matter for third-period totals.
Whether period markets include OT or only regulation periods.

interactions.hypothesis: First-period goals depend on opening deployments and goalie state; interacting opening shift lines with starting goalie quality is more informative than team-level rates.
Third-period totals and winners depend on game-script mixture: probability of being tied or trailing late times pull timing.
Second-period outcomes combine long-change effect with team skating depth and line shuffle tendencies.

first_event.target: Which team scores first, whether a goal is scored within the first N minutes, or related first-event contracts.
first_event.mechanism: Time to first goal is governed by the combined scoring hazard of both teams during the opening minutes, modulated by opening lines, early power plays and goalie quality; the first-scorer team is a race between two hazards, tilted by home ice and goalie/skater quality, with a first-period PP draw as a major random factor.

inputs.why: Direct early-game hazard estimates by team.
Team chance creation drives hazard.
Opponent suppression reduces hazard.
Goalie quality changes early goals against.
Starting units and early-shift line usage.
Early power play opportunities.
Early penalties give early PP.
High pace shortens expected time to first goal.
What counts as first goal and whether disallowed or empty-net goals count.

interactions.hypothesis: First-goal team probability depends on relative hazards, which depend on goalie quality interacting with opponent shot quality in the first period.
Pace and penalty tendencies interact: fast games with high early penalty rates produce early goals via PP.

player_points.target: Player goals, assists or points (thresholds like 1+ or 2+ points) in a game, with possible void on DNP.
player_points.mechanism: Points are rare events driven by the number of chances a player is on the ice for (TOI by strength state), the shooter/passer role on those chances (PP unit slot, linemates), the quality of those chances (xG), conversion luck, and the opponent's goal prevention including the starting goalie. Distribution is highly discrete and overdispersed, with most mass at 0 and a thin tail, so role and TOI information and regression of luck dominate.

inputs.why: TOI by state is the volume multiplier.
PP1 slot drives a disproportionate share of points.
Linemates define who converts passes and shoots.
Shot-quality-based scoring baseline for goals.
Individual shot volume for goal probability.
Playmaking role for assist markets.
Persistent finishing skill after regression.
On-ice conversion luck for assist and point projection.
Linemate finishing quality for assists and points.
Opposing goalie quality affects conversion rates.
Opponent suppression by position.
Lineup news changes linemates and PP roles.
If the player is scratched the contract may void rather than lose, which changes the price of a pregame position.
Count distribution for thresholds.
Correlated rungs on the player's ladder.
Returning players often carry reduced minutes and altered PP roles in their first games back.
Morning-skate lines and PP units arrive before official lineups and shift role expectations.
Matchup deployment against shutdown lines changes a star player scoring opportunities at home or away.

interactions.hypothesis: Points per game scale with TOI by state times per-minute rate: PP minutes and EV minutes need separate rates and the PP slot interacts with opponent PK structure.
Assist projection should use linemates' ixG-based finishing rather than realised on-ice SH%, because on-ice luck regresses.
A starting goalie change shifts every skater's goal probability, so the opposing goalie interacts with the player's ixG baseline.

player_shots.target: Player shots on goal in a game (threshold ladder), settled on official SOG counts.
player_shots.mechanism: SOG = TOI by strength state x attempts per minute x share of attempts reaching the net. Role (D vs F, PP slot, shooting-first players), game script (score effects), opponent block/suppression and rink counting bias determine the mean; variance is high because both TOI and shot rate fluctuate, and thresholds at 2-4 SOG fall in the dense part of the distribution.

inputs.why: Individual SOG rate per 60 is the central skill.
Minutes by state multiply shot rate.
PP time yields high shot rates for shooters.
Attempt-to-SOG conversion by shooter and opponent.
Opponent's shots allowed by position.
Opponent team shots volume allowed.
Rink scorer bias for SOG counting.
Trailing and leading change shot volume.
Probability of being in trailing states.
Linemates and zone deployment set how many attempts the player gets per shift.
A teammate's absence promotes the player to PP1 or a top line, raising shot volume sharply.
Defencemen shot counts come from point shots and PP time, with different volume and block rates than forwards.
Distribution for rung probabilities.
Correlated shot rungs for same player.
Call-ups change line composition and PP units, changing shot opportunities for regulars.
Returning players have reduced TOI so shots are below baseline for early games back.

interactions.hypothesis: SOG rate per minute depends on strength state: expected SOG is EV TOI x EV rate + PP TOI x PP rate, and projected PP TOI itself depends on penalty rates and crew.
Opponent block rate converts attempts into SOG differently for defencemen at the point and for forwards in the slot.
Trailing script raises shot volume for the underdog's stars and lowers favourites' late shots, so pregame win probability interacts with player TOI and shot rate.

goalie_saves.target: Goalie saves in a game (threshold ladder), requiring the goalie to play, settled on official save counts.
goalie_saves.mechanism: Saves = shots on goal faced minus goals allowed. Shots faced are determined by the opponent's attempts and SOG rates against this defence, with score-state effects (trailing team shoots more); goals allowed lower saves slightly. Early pulls truncate counts. Mean is driven by opposing volume and shot environment, variance by script and pull risk.

inputs.why: Expected SOG faced from team-level shot suppression.
Opponent shot creation volume and quality.
Total event volume of the game is the base for the number of shots the goalie can face.
Eligibility: market settlement depends on goalie playing.
Backup/starter probability and rest.
An early pull truncates the saves count and creates a lower tail not captured by a mean model.
Trailing opponents shoot more.
Win probability tilts shot volume.
PP chances for the opponent raise shots.
Official SOG counting bias at the rink moves the number of saves credited directly.
Opponent shooting by player mix.
Higher quality reduces goals and increases saves for given shots.
Shots faced are overdispersed; rung probabilities need a calibrated count distribution, not a mean.
Void/settlement rules when goalie does not start or is pulled.
First goalie off the ice at morning skate is a pregame tell for the starter and thus eligibility.

interactions.hypothesis: Saves distribution is a mixture over starter identity and pull events: P(starter) x saves distribution given starter, with pull risk truncating the upper tail.
Opponent SOG volume depends on game script: strong favourite goalies face fewer shots when team leads, so win probability interacts with shot volume against.
Special teams matter via both PP shots against and PK blocking: the penalties interaction with opponent PP shot volume shifts saves.

player_other.target: Head-to-head player comparisons (who records more points/shots) and other non-standard player markets.
player_other.mechanism: A head-to-head comparison is the difference of two correlated count processes: each player's expected output given role and matchup, with correlation from shared game environment (both on the same team or opposing teams) and tie handling defined by the rule. The distribution of the difference is wider than either marginal alone and tie/push rules matter.

inputs.why: Relative minutes of the two players.
Per-60 rates drive comparison for shot markets.
Relative PP roles decide which player collects the high-yield minutes that separate two similar skaters.
Linemates and deployment differences.
Difference in chance quality gives the expected gap in goals/points between the two players.
Differential opponent suppression.
Correlation shapes the difference distribution.
Lineup availability for either player.
If either player is scratched the comparison may void or settle against him depending on the wording.
Tie and DNP rules for the comparison.

interactions.hypothesis: For teammates, correlation via shared game script reduces variance of the difference; for opponents, scripts can produce negatively correlated shot volumes.
Difference of expected points depends on both players' PP roles and the opponent's penalty exposure, so PP minute distribution interacts with role.

combo.target: Multi-leg parlay/combo contracts across game outcome and player/team stats in one or more games.
combo.mechanism: A combo's probability is the joint probability of its legs, not the product of marginals: legs share latent drivers (pace, script, goalie, injuries) so correlation can be strongly positive (team win and player points) or negative. Pricing quality depends on marginal accuracy plus a correct joint structure.

inputs.why: The product of leg prices ignores correlation; a joint structure is required to price the combination.
Each leg needs a calibrated marginal count distribution before correlations are applied.
Shared script drives co-movement.
Shared goalie shock across legs.
A single lineup shock (star scratched) moves several legs at once and in related directions.
Team scoring level is the common latent driver of team-win, total and player-points legs.
Total and team-goal correlation.
How each leg settles and whether void legs reduce the combo.
Leg-level prices and cross-leg consistency.

interactions.hypothesis: A team win leg and a star player's points leg are positively correlated through team goals; conditioning on the game total and the team's goal expectation sets the joint probability.
Goalie shock hits all legs: a backup goalie raises opponent scoring legs, lowers own win legs, and raises totals together.

season_outcome.target: Season-level outcomes: championship, conference/division titles, playoff qualification, playoff series winners.
season_outcome.mechanism: These markets integrate team strength over many games or a short series: probability is the result of a simulation using team ratings with their uncertainty, injuries, schedule, tiebreakers and bracket structure. Futures are heavily influenced by rating uncertainty and by information that arrives slowly (injuries, trades), and hold time of capital matters.

inputs.why: Calibrated team strength with uncertainty.
Process-based offence component of ratings.
Process-based defence component.
Goalie is the largest single-player driver, especially in playoffs.
Long-term injuries to stars change strength.
Remaining schedule difficulty and games in hand.
Qualification and seeding in tight races are decided by formal tie-break order, not raw points.
Series state for playoff series markets.
Lucky shooting/save runs inflate standings; regress before simulating the rest of the season.
Playoff-specific TOI and penalty environment.
Trades, coaching changes and signings shift team strength after public ratings were fitted.
Sportsbook futures prices are a benchmark for rating-based probabilities and show the market's information.

interactions.hypothesis: Playoff odds depend on rating uncertainty: with the same mean strength, higher uncertainty helps underdogs in short series; simulate with correlated rating errors.
Goalie quality is the most volatile determinant in playoffs; a goalie change interacts with the process rating to move series odds more than skater changes.
Standing luck (PDO and OT record) mean-reverts, but qualification depends on the tie-break structure, so regress then apply formal rules.

season_stat.target: Season-total or leader outcomes for players or teams (goals, points, saves, wins), settled at end of season or on specified date.
season_stat.mechanism: Cumulative stats equal rate x opportunity: rest-of-season per-game production times expected games played, with health risk and role changes. Leader markets also depend on competitors' paths and the top-tail variance of counts.

inputs.why: To-date totals and rest-of-season projection.
A recent TOI or role change shifts the rest-of-season rate before season totals reveal it.
PP role is a stable scoring driver.
Chance-quality baseline separates sustainable production from finishing luck in the rest-of-season rate.
Hot shooting that exceeds skill regresses, lowering the rest-of-season projection for current leaders.
Games missed to injury directly reduce totals and change leader probabilities.
Age curve gives a prior for rate changes and for the injury hazard over the remaining season.
Games remaining and opponent quality set opportunity count and chance quality for the rest of the season.
Distribution of totals for thresholds.
Trades or role changes alter opportunity and linemates for the player mid-season.

interactions.hypothesis: Projected total = games remaining x health probability x per-game rate; the injury hazard interacts with age and workload.
Leader races are decided by top-tail variance of rate and by role stability, so TOI trend interacts with PP role.

season_award.target: Winners (or finalists) of league awards such as Hart, Vezina, Norris, Calder, Selke, Conn Smythe, decided by voters.
season_award.mechanism: Award outcomes are a mixture of measurable production and voter narrative, filtered through ballot structure and timing; the best predictor is a voter-behaviour model fit on historical finalists with stats, team success and position. Late-season injuries and finalist announcements are discrete information events.

inputs.why: Counting stats and advanced metrics voters see.
Who votes, how many ballot slots and when ballots are cast determine which information can matter.
Team success correlates with winning.
Goalie awards depend on save percentage and workload.
Narrative around rookies and age curves influence voters for Calder and comeback-style awards.
Games played and late injuries.
Late narrative events (injury, milestone, scandal) can swing voters, especially before ballot deadlines.
Finalist announcements and the award date define when information resolves and when markets can close.

interactions.hypothesis: Voter models combine production rank and team rank: a candidate on a high-seeded team with top-two production has a higher chance than raw rank implies.
Finalist announcements and ballot deadlines create step changes: late-season injuries after ballots close do not affect votes.

off_field.target: Non-game events (trades, coaching, league announcements, business or non-hockey questions) settled by public announcement.
off_field.mechanism: These markets depend on organizational decisions and news flow rather than on-ice performance; there is no strong statistical model, so the best hypotheses are reference-class frequencies, calendar constraints, insider reports and the exact resolution wording. Largely unpredictable from hockey statistics.

inputs.why: Reference-class frequency of the same type of announcement is the best available prior for novelty markets.
Fixed league dates bound when the event can occur and concentrate hazard near them.
Insider reports often precede official announcements; timing and reliability of reports drive repricing.
Resolution wording and source.
Market-implied probability and news timing.
Thin liquidity means the quoted probability is noisy and sparse trading limits the value of any signal.
Market open/close timing relative to events.
Other venue prices where they exist.

interactions.hypothesis: Base rate adjusted by calendar: probability concentrates in dated windows, so reference-class frequency interacts with time to deadline.
Insider-report timing leads official announcement; price reaction after reports shows information content and the rule defines what counts.

player_points_goals_assists.label: Skater goals / assists / points thresholds
player_points_goals_assists.target: Whether a skater records at least k goals, assists or points in the game (typically 1+, 2+, 3+), subject to the contract's DNP rule.
player_points_goals_assists.mechanism: Each goal is a Bernoulli outcome on every shot, so goals follow from shots x shot quality x finishing x opposing goalie; assists require being the passer on a teammate goal and so depend on linemates' finishing and on the player's playmaking role. Points are the union, so volume (TOI, especially PP1 time) dominates, while on-ice shooting luck is noise. The distribution is zero-heavy with thin tails, so thresholds above 1 need joint information on game total and team goals.

inputs.why: Minutes by EV/PP/PK are the volume multiplier; projected from the confirmed lineup and expected script.
PP1 vs PP2 membership and slot (shooter, quarterback, bumper) produces most of the variance between similarly rated players.
Individual xG/60 is the lowest-noise baseline for goals; regress to finishing-adjusted level.
Primary assist rate is the skill-linked part; secondary assists should be given little persistence.
Linemates' shot quality and finishing determine conversion of the player's passes.
Strips lucky/unlucky on-ice shooting%; regress to xG-implied value.
Persistent finishing talent after shrinkage separates elite shooters from average.
Opposing starter identity shifts goal probability for all skaters; confirmation timing matters.
Opponent suppression by position adjusts shot volume and chance quality.
Opponent PK shape determines PP unit effectiveness.
Expected opponent penalties set the player's PP minutes.
Crew effect on number of penalties called, small but scaled to PP-heavy players.
Absences promote or demote players to PP1/top lines; late scratches settle or void per rules.
Expected total and team goals scale all team skater outcomes.
Zero-inflated/NB shape needed to translate mean to threshold probability.
DNP treatment changes effective probability.
Goals/assists/points ladders for a player are nested and correlated.
Counts of empty-net goals, OT and shootout goals vary by wording.
Provides the stable credit share that converts team scoring into points and assists; absent from the draft which relied on raw assist rate and finishing.
Linemate and role effects on points and assists enter the model as a measurable on-ice chance-creation rate.
Supplies the competing-risk structure for the first-goal contract, which is not a simple ladder rung.
Explains late-game point production beyond the 5v5 and PP model and helps the multi-point rungs.
Converts injury news into the specific promoted player's minutes, the key personnel effect in prop ladders.
Skater production on the power play is limited by the first-unit share and termination of minors on a goal; PP1 membership is worth more than raw PP minutes.
Gives the contract a market-free script latent (state mixture and entering-state matrix) so that benchmark prices remain an independent yardstick.
Provides the only defined input chain for KXNHLF10G, a team-pair early-goal event with a half-open 0:00 to 10:00 window.
Captures the overtime 3v3 exposure that the single-game ladders and first-goal contract can include but the record omitted.
Opportunity cap for all player season counting contracts, and the source of the left tail of the goal total.
Gives the season-points contracts a market-free chain (rate, role, games played) instead of leaving them to a single-game or goals-only mechanism.

interactions.hypothesis: PP minutes x PP point rate x opponent PK structure: expected PP production is the product of unit share of PP time, projected penalties drawn, and the PK concession pattern, not any one of them.
Assists = linemates' conversion x player's primary-assist rate; regress on-ice SH% before use, so linemate xG interacts with on-ice luck regression.
Goal probability = ixG-based chance volume x finishing x opponent goalie quality adjustments; goalie danger-split matters most for shooters of high-danger shots.
Multi-point thresholds are driven by team-level goal environment: team total and empty-net share raise the odds that the star is on ice for several goals.

PP production is the product of the unit's share of power-play time, penalties drawn and PK concession, and unit share is front-loaded while a goal ends the penalty, so extra penalty minutes yield fewer extra PP1 chances than the product of averages suggests.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate PP points per PP opportunity against PP seconds elapsed and compare with a time x rate model for PP1 and PP2 skaters.

interactions.hypothesis: Expected points are on-ice goals for times the skater's credit share; a player with average individual shooting but elite linemates and high IPP outproduces what ixG says, and the two factors multiply rather than add.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress points per game on log on-ice xGF and log IPP and compare to an additive model on holdout seasons.

interactions.hypothesis: The 2+ and 3+ rungs scale convexly with team goals: a three-point game requires team goals of at least two and the star on ice for most of them, so a rise in team total lifts P(3+) several times faster than P(1+).
interactions.how_to_test: Compute P(points>=k) by team goal bins and fit the elasticity of each rung to team goals.

interactions.hypothesis: An absence only helps the next man if he inherits power-play slots, not just even-strength minutes; the promotion of a depth forward to PP1 changes his point rate by a multiple while an even-strength promotion changes it little.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare production of promoted players across promotions that include versus exclude PP1 time.

interactions.hypothesis: First goalscorer requires a first goal at all and an early power play makes the scorer drawn from PP1; the early penalty process and the scorer share interact, so top-line shares at 5v5 understate the first-goal chances of PP1 players.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute player first-goal share separately for first goals scored on the power play versus even strength.

nonlinearities.shape: Saturating: P(goal>=1) = 1 - exp(-lambda)
nonlinearities.why: At lambda about 0.3 the probability is about 26 percent, and each added 0.1 of expected goals adds less than the one before; linear features on ixG overstate the high-end players and understate the 2+ rung.

nonlinearities.shape: Piecewise: power-play minutes weigh more than even-strength minutes
nonlinearities.why: A minute on the power play carries roughly two to three times the scoring rate of an even-strength minute, and blowout compression cuts even-strength minutes but not PP minutes, so total TOI is a poor linear predictor.

nonlinearities.shape: Zero-inflated count with thin right tail
nonlinearities.why: Assist counts have a mass at zero larger than Poisson and heavier tails when the team scores many goals; threshold rungs at 2+ and 3+ are sensitive to this shape more than to the mean.

mechanism_review.summary: A skater's goals, assists and points in a game are counts accumulated only while he is on the ice and credited by the scorer. First, availability and role decide whether he plays and where: line, power-play unit, penalty kill. Second, minutes by strength state set the number of opportunities, with power-play time the most valuable and the most uncertain because it depends on penalties called. Third, goals follow from shots times shot quality times finishing against the opposing goalie, with P(at least one) saturating as the mean grows. Fourth, assists and points depend on how often the player is credited on goals his team scores while he is on the ice (individual points percentage), which depends on role: forwards on scoring lines have high shares, defencemen lower. Fifth, the team's goal environment scales everything, so multi-point rungs are driven by team total and by whether the star is on the ice for several of them.

stages.name: Availability, lineup slot and replacement redistribution
stages.description: Whether the skater plays and in which slot is the first stage: a skater who is active but never enters settles at the last fair price, while a healthy scratch or pregame injury has no stated treatment (pp5), and teammates' absences promote players to the top line or the first power-play unit. A player's ceiling in the game depends on who replaces whom, and promotions are partially known from morning skate and partially only at warmups. The replacement pattern determines minutes and linemates, so it propagates into every later stage.
stages.distribution: Discrete lineup scenarios per team; each scenario sets a TOI and unit assignment with different means.

stages.name: Time on ice and power-play volume
stages.description: Minutes are split into even strength, power play and penalty kill, and roughly a third of a top forward's scoring comes on the power play in few minutes. PP minutes depend on the number of penalties the opponent takes (random) and on the unit's share of each power play, which is front-loaded because a minor ends on a goal. Blowouts compress the stars' minutes and late-game extra-attacker deployment adds a small block of minutes to specific players.
stages.distribution: Minutes: roughly normal at even strength with sd of 2-3 minutes; PP minutes compound (Poisson penalties times unit share) with heavy right tail.

stages.name: Shot generation, shot quality and finishing for goals
stages.description: Goals per game follow from shot attempts, on-target share, location quality and the skater's finishing, against the opposing starting goalie. The individual expected-goals rate per 60 is the most stable baseline; finishing talent varies and is shrunk hard. P(at least one goal) = 1 - exp(-lambda) saturates, so a doubling of the mean does not double the probability, while the 2+ and 3+ rungs depend on the tail of a count with lambda of 0.3-0.5 for top scorers. The skater shot volume enters explicitly through nhl.shot_rate (shot attempts and shots on goal per 60 by state), not only implicitly through ixG.
stages.distribution: Poisson or zero-inflated count of goals with lambda about 0.1-0.5; P(2+) about an order of magnitude below P(1+).

stages.name: Assist and point credit on team goals
stages.description: Points are credited on goals scored while the player is on the ice: a team goal gives a point to the scorer and up to two assists, and the individual points percentage (his points divided by on-ice goals for) is a stable role-dependent share. Expected points = on-ice goal exposure x IPP, where the exposure combines team quality on the ice and linemate finishing, and secondary assists are noisy. This makes assists and points more dependent on teammates than goals, and correlates assists with the team's goal environment.
stages.distribution: Credit structure: each goal yields 1 goal + 0-2 assists (about 12-15 percent unassisted); assists/points are compound counts with higher correlation to team goals than individual goals.

stages.name: Team goal environment and special settlement variants
stages.description: The team's goals scored scale every skater-level count: a team with an expected three goals gives its top line roughly 3x more chances for a multi-point night than a team with two, and game total and script (blowout, empty-net) correlate players across a team. KXNHLFIRSTGOAL is different in kind: a competing-risk race in which the player's share of his team's goal hazard times P(his team scores first) gives his probability, with a separate 'No Goalscorer' outcome when regulation and overtime are scoreless (shootout goals excluded); KXNHLANYGOAL (title only) is presumed to be the 1+ rung of the goal chain, unverified (pp1).
stages.distribution: Team goals ~ NB with mean 2.6-3.4; first-goal timing roughly exponential with mean of order 10-12 minutes (to be measured).

environment.note: A skater's single-game goal and assist counts are not affected by weather or altitude in an indoor rink; rink scoring and recording factors act through team rates, which are captured by the opposing team and goalie inputs.

coaching_scheme.note: Coach effects on skater production act through TOI, PP unit assignment and line combinations, which are modelled directly as role inputs; no separate coach-level feature adds information beyond those slots for single-game ladders.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Rest and standings stakes affect whether stars play, which is captured by availability and next-man-up inputs; the residual effect on per-minute production of a skater who plays is negligible.

required_data.dataset: Goal events with scorer, assists and on-ice skaters
required_data.timestamp_requirement: Event time and credit as recorded; keep corrections vintage.
required_data.history_needed: 2007-08 onward for credits; 2012-13 onward for xG.

candidate_sources.name: NHL API play-by-play
candidate_sources.note: goals with scorer and assists, on-ice skater ids

required_data.dataset: Player-game TOI by state, lines and PP units

contract_review.settlement_definition: KXNHLGOAL, KXNHLAST and KXNHLPTS are ladders of 'N+' contracts (sampled strikes: 1.5 on assists, 2.5 on goals and points; the 0.5 rung is inferred, not seen) that pay YES if the named skater records at least that many in the listed game; if the player is active but never enters the game the market settles to the last fair market price before game start, and once he enters it settles on the stat recorded. KXNHLFIRSTGOAL pays if the named player scores the first goal of the game (regulation or overtime, shootout goals excluded) with a separate No Goalscorer market. KXNHLANYGOAL is title-only. None of the ladder texts says whether overtime or empty-net goals count; official box-score credit is assumed.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official NHL box score and play-by-play game summary for goals, assists and points.
variants_and_edge_cases: Ladder nesting: 1+, 2+, 3+ rungs on goals, assists and points are nested events; points rungs also nest goals and assists (points >= goals), so rung probabilities for one player must be mutually consistent.
KXNHLANYGOAL is title-only (no markets listed): whether empty-net and overtime goals count, and how the market differs from the N+ ladder, is unseen and marked CONTRACT_AMBIGUOUS.

Reconciled series: KXNHLF10G (either-team early goal) moved to game_events and KXNHLSEASONPPTS (season points) to the season-counting archetype; the single-game skater chain here no longer carries them.
Official scoring credit can be revised after the game (assists, goal attribution), so the data version used for settlement matters; the sampled text does not say which feed is authoritative.

player_shots_on_goal.label: Skater shots on goal thresholds
player_shots_on_goal.target: Whether a skater records at least k official shots on goal in the game.
player_shots_on_goal.mechanism: Shots on goal result from TOI by state times attempt rate times the fraction of attempts that are not blocked or missed. Role differences are large: forwards in the slot, defencemen at the point and PP1 shooters generate shots at very different rates per minute, and the count is overdispersed because script, penalties and linemates change both volume and accuracy. Official counting varies by rink, so venue bias is a direct measurement effect on settlement.

inputs.why: SOG/60 by strength state is the core rate; EWMA with shrinkage and linemate adjustment.
Projected EV/PP minutes from lineup; blowouts change TOI.
PP shooter slot yields much higher shot rates per minute than EV.
SOG/attempt conversion depends on shooter and opponent block rates.
D-man SOG is point-shot based and PP-dependent.
Position-specific opponent shots allowed.
Opponent's shot volume allowed overall.
Scorer counting bias changes official SOG at some arenas.
Trailing teams shoot more; leading teams shoot less late.
Win probability and expected total change script.
Penalty expectation sets PP shot opportunities.
Linemates and zone deployment affect shot share.
Offensive-zone usage lifts attempts per minute.
Recent role changes before season averages catch up.
Lineup news changes TOI and role; late scratch handled by settlement rule.
NB shape for rung probabilities.
Shot rungs share the same latent mean; stale rungs are detectable.
Danger-zone versus perimeter shot mix separates volume shooters from high-quality shooters and shows whether opponents force low-value shots on goal.
Separates team-level volume from the skater's role share so lineup changes and opponent volume are handled correctly.
Gives the exact change in the listed skater's SOG expectation from teammate absences, which matter more in this market than the injury flag itself.
Shots on the power play are concentrated in the first unit's initial seconds and the penalty ends on a goal, so PP shots per penalty is concave in minutes and PP1 shooters dominate.
Official SOG is a scorer-recorded count, so any arena-level recording factor shifts counts directly for thresholds, and the claim must be tested before being used.
If overtime counts, 3v3 produces several shots for top skaters in a short period and shifts the 4+ rungs for stars in games with high tie probability.
Gives the contract a market-free script latent (state mixture and entering-state matrix) so that benchmark prices remain an independent yardstick.

interactions.hypothesis: Expected SOG = EV TOI x EV rate + PP TOI x PP rate; PP TOI is uncertain because it depends on the number of penalties drawn, so PP-heavy shooters have fatter right tails.
Block/miss conversion x shooter type: defencemen face higher block rates at the point and forwards' SOG depend on slot volume, so the opponent block rate has different effects by position.
Rink counting bias scales official SOG for both teams; adjust the player's rate by home/away venue factor, interacting with the player's home share.
Script x TOI: for a favoured team's star, leading late reduces minutes and shots; for an underdog star, trailing raises both.

Expected SOG rises with the number of power plays, and PP1 shooters convert minutes to shots at several times the even-strength rate, so uncertainty in penalty counts fattens the right tail for PP1 shooters but not for penalty-kill defencemen.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute realised SOG for PP1 shooters by number of power plays in the game and compare with depth forwards.

interactions.hypothesis: Blocks reduce defencemen's point shots far more than forwards' slot shots, so an opponent with strong blocking suppresses defencemen's SOG more; the opponent block rate should be applied conditional on position and shot origin.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate opponent block rate coefficients separately for forwards and defencemen in an attempts-to-SOG model.

interactions.hypothesis: Expected SOG equals team volume times the player's share of volume; a high-share forward against a defence that allows few shots has a mean far below his season average, and share and team volume are not additive.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare predictions from team-volume x share against a per-60 rate model on out-of-sample games.

interactions.hypothesis: When the unit's high-volume shooter is absent, remaining skaters' shares rise by the vacated amount in proportion to their usage; the effect is conditional on who is out and on whether the replacement is a shooter or a passer.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate share change for linemates by absent-player type in games with and without that player.

interactions.hypothesis: Stars on the leading team lose minutes only when the lead reaches about three goals; below that threshold their shot count is unaffected, while trailing teams' stars add shots late, so the response of SOG to lead is a threshold, not linear.
interactions.how_to_test: Bin by final goal difference and compare TOI and SOG of top-line skaters on winning versus losing teams.

interactions.hypothesis: If an arena records shots more generously, the effect scales with the number of attempts that reach the net and applies to home and visiting skaters alike, so it multiplies the player rate rather than adding a constant; the effect should be larger for high-volume shooters.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit the arena random effect on visiting-team skater SOG per 60 and test whether the effect scales with the player baseline rate (log-link slope near one) rather than being additive.

nonlinearities.shape: Negative binomial: tail grows with the mean convexly
nonlinearities.why: For a mean of 2.8 the probability of 4+ is about a quarter and of 5+ a tenth, and these rungs are far more sensitive to dispersion than 1+ or 2+, so a Poisson assumption misprices high rungs.

nonlinearities.shape: Piecewise linear with PP minutes carrying a higher slope
nonlinearities.why: A power-play minute yields two to three times the SOG of an even-strength minute, so total TOI is a poor linear predictor and the minutes must be split by state.

nonlinearities.shape: Saturating conversion bounded between 0 and 1
nonlinearities.why: Attempt-to-SOG conversion cannot exceed one and varies in a narrow band, so improvements in volume translate to SOG linearly but differences in block rate apply multiplicatively.

mechanism_review.summary: A skater's recorded shots on goal are the output of four multiplicative stages. Exposure: whether he plays and for how many minutes in each strength state, with power-play time the highest-rate minutes. Volume: his attempt rate per minute, which depends on role (forward in the slot, defenceman at the point, PP1 shooter), on linemates who compete for the same shots, and on the team's overall volume against this opponent. Conversion: the fraction of attempts that reach the net rather than being blocked or missing the target, which differs sharply by position and by the opponent's blocking tendency. Counting: the official scorer's decisions. The count is overdispersed because script, penalties and linemate changes move volume and accuracy together, and ladders at 3+ or 4+ sit in the tail for most skaters, so the mean and the dispersion jointly determine rung probabilities.

stages.name: Availability and role slot
stages.description: Shots depend on whether the skater plays, which line he is on, and whether he holds a first power-play unit slot; a promoted depth forward or a returning star changes his role within a game, and an injury during the game truncates exposure. Lineup is fixed mostly at warmups, and replacement of a teammate redistributes shot opportunities inside the line and the unit, so the player's expected volume must be updated when linemates change.
stages.distribution: Discrete lineup scenarios per team; within each, an exposure mean and a probability of mid-game truncation of order 1-2 percent.

stages.name: Minutes by strength state
stages.description: Expected SOG equals even-strength minutes times the even-strength SOG rate plus power-play minutes times the much higher PP rate. Power-play minutes depend on penalties the opponent takes and on the unit's share of each power play, and blowouts compress stars' even-strength minutes. Projected TOI by state is therefore the basic scale of the count and has a heavy right tail from extra power plays.
stages.distribution: Minutes roughly normal at even strength (sd 2-3 min) and compound-Poisson on the power play; PP minutes are highest-variance.

stages.name: Attempt volume and shot-share within the unit
stages.description: Attempt rate per minute reflects role: forwards who play in the slot and take rebounds, defencemen shooting from the point, and PP shooters; it varies with linemates because shot shares sum within a unit, and with the opponent's suppression of volume. Expressing volume as a share of team shots while on ice and multiplying by team volume stabilises estimates, as shares persist more than raw per-60 rates.
stages.distribution: Overdispersed count (negative binomial) with a skater-specific mean of 1.5-4 and variance about 1.3-1.8 times the mean.

stages.name: Attempt-to-SOG conversion and official counting
stages.description: Only unblocked, on-target attempts are shots on goal: defencemen's point shots are blocked more often, forwards in the slot are blocked less but miss more often, and opposing teams differ in blocking. After conversion, the official scorer applies the definition, and arenas can differ in how generously they record. The threshold contract then reads the count at k.
stages.distribution: Binomial thinning of attempts with success probability about 0.5-0.65 (position dependent); recording noise adds a small additional variance.

settlement_contract.note: No rules text exists for this archetype (NO_LIVE_SERIES): settlement mechanics are only the assumed official-SOG recording and OT counting, covered conditionally by these two inputs; the actual contract wording is the open item sg1.

officiating_rules.note: Referee crew affects the number of power plays, which is already inside the penalty input and the power-play minutes stage; apart from that, the scorer's counting decision is the only officiating effect and is handled as an arena recording factor.

coaching_scheme.note: Coach influence on a single skater's shots arrives through line combinations, power-play unit and minutes, all of which are modelled directly; no additional coach-level term is separately identifiable for a single-game count.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Fatigue and standings stakes act through lineup decisions and minutes, which the TOI and availability inputs already carry; the per-minute shot rate of a player who plays is not materially changed by schedule.

contract_review.settlement_definition: No live Kalshi series exists for NHL skater shots on goal, so there is no rules text. The blueprint assumes an 'N+ shots on goal' ladder analogous to the live KXNHLGOAL, KXNHLAST and KXNHLPTS ladders, settling on the official recorded shots on goal for the named skater in the listed game; by analogy a skater who is active but never enters would settle at the last fair price, and whether overtime shots and shootout attempts count would need to be read from the actual rules when a series lists. All of this is an inference from sibling contracts, not observed text.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Assumed: official NHL box score player shots on goal (the NHL stats API exposes player shot counts in the boxscore; SOURCE_UNVERIFIED for field naming and revision behaviour).
variants_and_edge_cases: Official SOG definition: shots that are saved or score are recorded by the league scorer; blocked shots and misses are not shots on goal, so the settlement depends on the scorer's judgement and on the recording practice of the arena.

Overtime and shootout: 3v3 overtime shots are ordinary game shots and plausibly count, whereas shootout attempts are not counted in official SOG; neither is confirmed by any rules text for this archetype.

Ladder construction by analogy: nested thresholds (1+, 2+, 3+, 4+, ...) with a monotone probability curve, so the rungs for one player must be mutually consistent and ladder consistency can be used only as a diagnostic.

Player status: active-but-never-enters, healthy scratch and mid-game injury (a player leaves after one shift) lead to different realised counts; the sibling rule would settle the first case at fair price and the last on counted shots.

goalie_saves.label: Goalie saves thresholds
goalie_saves.target: Whether a goalie records at least k saves; eligibility conditional on the goalie playing per the wording.
goalie_saves.mechanism: Saves equal shots on goal faced minus goals against, so the mean is the opponent's expected SOG against this defence adjusted for script, penalties and rink counting. Goalie quality only matters at the margin (a few shots), while volume matters most. The largest tail risks are an early pull (truncating saves) and goalie identity uncertainty before confirmation; overtime adds shots if included.

Directly forecasts the number of shots the goalie will see, which is the main variance driver of saves.
Turns 'goalie plays' into the precise exposure distribution that determines the lower tail and the settlement mixture of this contract.
Tests the draft's claim that rink counting bias is a primary driver of saves; if the factor is under two percent the input is dropped.
Provides the OT contribution to a threshold that sits near the median where a few shots matter.
Gives the contract a market-free script latent (state mixture and entering-state matrix) so that benchmark prices remain an independent yardstick.

interactions.hypothesis: Saves mean = expected SOG faced x (1 - expected goal probability), but variance is dominated by shot volume and pull risk; combine volume distribution with pull mixture.
Favourite goalies: strong teams concede fewer shots and may lead late; interacting win probability with opponent shooting volume tilts the mean down for favourites.
Unconfirmed starter: the ladder is a mixture across starters with different expected volume (starters vs backup facing the same team), so price jumps on confirmation.
Rink SOG counting bias and opponent attempt volume jointly set official shots faced; venue effects matter more for high-volume opponents.

Expected shots faced is the product of the opponent's shot generation and this defence's allowance, with power-play time as an additional multiplier because PP shot rates are about double 5v5; a high-shot opponent facing a leaky penalty-prone defence compounds all three.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit log SOG with offence, defence and penalty-minute terms and test their products against the additive model.

interactions.hypothesis: Saves have a different relationship to shots in the full-game and pulled regimes: a pull after four goals truncates the count well below the rung, so the distribution below 25 is a mixture whose weight depends on early goals allowed, and goalie quality moves the pull weight rather than the mean.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare saves distributions conditional on first-period goals against (0 to 3+) and fit the mixture weight against goalie save rate.

interactions.hypothesis: Before confirmation the model distribution of saves is a mixture over the two possible goalies; if the backup would face the same volume the mean barely changes and only the save rate differs by tenths of a percentage point, so the confirmation effect is smaller than for goal markets.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare the model mixture before confirmation with the single-goalie distribution after confirmation on games where the starter changed; use Kalshi price paths only as an external yardstick for reaction timing, never as a model input.

interactions.hypothesis: Overtime adds a block of shots only when regulation is tied, which shifts the mean by about one shot weighted by the tie probability but moves the probability of crossing 25 more when the base mean is near 24; the effect is largest at the median rung.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress realised crossing of the 25-save rung on regulation saves and an OT indicator and compare to the model prediction.

interactions.hypothesis: A favourite faces fewer shots at even strength because it controls play, but score effects work in the opposite direction once it leads: the trailing team shoots more and later pulls its goalie, so the leader's goalie faces the 6v5 flurry. The net shots-against edge of a favourite is therefore smaller than its shot-share gap and saturates beyond a two-goal lead, while underdog goalies carry more early-pull truncation risk.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress shots against on the simulated lead-time share and on team shot share separately, by period, and check that the third-period coefficient on leading is positive while the first-period coefficient on team strength is negative.

nonlinearities.shape: S-shaped (cumulative) response of P(25+) to the mean
nonlinearities.why: With sd of shots faced of 5-6 the probability of reaching 25 rises from about 20 to 80 percent as the mean moves from 21 to 29, so a small mean error near the rung causes large probability error.

nonlinearities.shape: Bimodal lower-tail mixture of full and pulled games
nonlinearities.why: A pull converts a typical 25-save game into a 12-18 save game; the saves distribution is a mixture, so a unimodal NB underestimates the mass far below the rung and overestimates it near the mean.

nonlinearities.shape: Saturating in lead size
nonlinearities.why: Shot suppression for the goalie on the leading team saturates after a two-goal lead since leaders play defensively but do not reduce further, while a trailing opponent's late 6v5 shots rise sharply near the end.

mechanism_review.summary: Saves equal shots on goal faced minus goals allowed, so the count is determined first by exposure (how many minutes the named goalie is in net, including the chance he is pulled or never plays), then by the shot flow the opponent produces against this defence, and last by a binomial thinning in which each shot becomes a goal with probability of roughly one in eleven to one in ten (to be measured by season). Volume dominates: the standard deviation of shots faced is several times larger than the effect of goalie skill, and the 25-save rung sits near the median for a typical starter so the probability is steep in the mean. Score effects redistribute shots by minute: trailing teams shoot more, and the trailing team pulls its goalie late, so it is the LEADING team's goalie who faces the 6v5 flurry while the trailing goalie is out of net with his count frozen; power plays concentrate shots. Settlement adds a regime: a dressed goalie who never enters pays at fair price, and a pull truncates the total.

stages.name: Exposure: who plays and for how many minutes
stages.description: The named goalie's saves accrue only while he is in net. Exposure is a mixture over start/no-start (a backup who dresses and does not play settles at the last fair price), full 60 minutes versus pulled after a goal burst, and overtime minutes. Back-to-back and recent workload determine start probability, morning-skate signals and team patterns refine it, and confirmation arrives close to puck drop. After a pull, the relief goalie has only a small partial exposure.
stages.distribution: Three-component mixture on minutes: ~0 (no entry, fair-price), partial (pulled at time T, usually after 3-4 goals), and full 60 (+ OT); pull probability roughly one start in ten.

stages.name: Opponent shot flow against this defence
stages.description: Shots on goal faced come from the opponent's attempt volume, the fraction that are on goal rather than blocked or missed, and this defence's suppression, shaped by score state and penalties: power plays generate roughly twice the shot rate of 5v5 and trailing teams shoot more. Opponent SOG-for per 60 by state and defence SOG-against by state combine log-additively; the league average in recent seasons is closer to 27-30 shots per team-game and must be measured per season (SOURCE_UNVERIFIED here). Overtime adds a short 3v3 high-event period. Direction of the favourite effect: a stronger team has a lower baseline shot share against its goalie, but score effects push the other way once it leads (the trailing team shoots more), so the net shots-against edge of a favourite is smaller than its shot-share gap and can reverse in the third period.
stages.distribution: Negative-binomial counts of shots faced with mean near the current-season league average (roughly 27-30, to be measured) and sd about 5-6 (overdispersed relative to Poisson because of PP and score-state clustering).

stages.name: Conversion: goals allowed thin the shot count
stages.description: Each shot becomes a goal with probability set by shot danger and the goalie's skill, so saves given shots are binomial with success probability near 0.9. A goalie of persistent skill moves this by a point or two; shot quality of the opponent mix (rebounds, rush chances) moves it similarly. Goals also change the game: more goals against shift the score state and raise pull risk, so saves and shots are negatively linked at the extremes.
stages.distribution: Binomial thinning of shots with p about 0.90; goals allowed approximately Poisson with mean 2.7-3.0; saves = shots minus goals.

stages.name: Official counting and settlement
stages.description: The recorded save count comes from the league scorer's shot-on-goal decisions, so rink-level recording differences enter directly, and from the treatment of OT and shootout shots, which official statistics handle differently. Because the contract is a threshold on a discrete count, the probability is the upper tail of the saves distribution at 25; ladders for the same goalie are nested rungs.
stages.distribution: Discrete count with threshold at k; probability steep in the mean (a one-save mean shift moves P(25+) by about 8-10 points).

environment.note: Arena SOG recording bias is carried by nhl.arena_sog_recording_factor; nhl.venue is audited as a duplicate, so no separate home-ice term is claimed here (home effect on saves is second-order).

coaching_scheme.note: No input captures the coach's decision rule for pulling a goalie after goals allowed or for scheduling starts (e.g. split starts, rest after a bad outing), which drives both exposure and the truncated lower tail.

contract_review.settlement_definition: KXNHLSAVE pays YES if the named goaltender records at least the stated number of saves (threshold 25+, floor_strike 24.5) in the listed NHL game. If the goalie is active but never enters the game the market settles to the last fair market price before game start, so a backup who dresses and does not play is a void-like fair-price outcome rather than NO; once he enters, the market settles on saves recorded. Whether overtime saves and shootout shots count, and what happens if the goalie is not on the active roster at all, is not stated in the sampled text.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official NHL box score goalie line (saves), as recorded by league scorers; fair-price rule determined by Kalshi.
variants_and_edge_cases: Pulled goalie: a starter replaced after four goals keeps the saves already recorded, so the lower tail below the rung is bimodal (full game vs early pull), and the backup who relieves has a separate small exposure.

Overtime: saves in the 5-minute 3v3 period are official goalie saves and plausibly count toward 'in the game', but the text does not say; shootout shots are not counted in official saves, an assumption the text does not confirm.
Active-but-never-enters versus scratched or not dressed: the text covers 'active' players only, so a goalie who is not on the game roster is a CONTRACT_AMBIGUOUS case (void, fair price or NO).
Strike construction is a single 25+ style contract per rung; rung ladder for a goalie is nested and monotone in the threshold, and the sampled strike is a one-sided 'at least' contract.

game_moneyline_puckline.label: Game winner, regulation winner, puck line and win margin
game_moneyline_puckline.target: Which team wins (including OT/SO or regulation only), covers a goal spread, or wins by a given margin.
game_moneyline_puckline.mechanism: Team goal differential is the difference of two overdispersed count processes with means set by team xG quality, goalie, special teams and home ice; moneyline including OT adds a near-coin-flip resolution of regulation ties, puck line and margin markets depend on the full goal-difference distribution (including the empty-net goal that pushes margin by one). The edge from public information is small because lines are efficient; value arises from fast reaction to goalie/lineup news and rule-structure differences across contracts.

interactions.hypothesis: Goalie confirmation x opponent shot-danger mix: the benefit of a better goalie is proportional to high-danger volume faced, so start news should be scaled by opponent profile.
Regulation-only vs including-OT prices differ by P(tie): the same rating gap implies different probabilities across contracts, so total and spread feed the tie model.
Puck-line cover depends on empty-net goals: a one-goal lead late converts to a two-goal win via EN, so pull timing interacts with game script.
Rest/back-to-back effect is mostly through backup goalie; condition the rest flag on starter identity before using it as an independent edge.

Goals saved above a replacement goalie scale with how many dangerous shots the opponent produces, so a backup start costs a high-volume attacking opponent more than a low-volume one; effect is proportional, not additive.
interactions.how_to_test: Interact goalie quality delta with opponent xG-for per 60 in a goal-difference regression and test the product term.

interactions.hypothesis: A one-goal lead past about three minutes triggers a pull and then a high chance of a two-goal margin; spread rungs at 1.5 and 2.5 respond to the leader's EN success and to the trailer's pull time, which are team specific.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare realised P(margin >= 2 | lead by 1 at 3:00) across teams grouped by 6v5 profile.

interactions.hypothesis: The 1.5 and 2.5 spread rungs depend on the expected goal gap relative to the spread of the difference, which grows with the expected total: the same rating gap yields a smaller margin-of-three probability in a low-event matchup than in a high-event one, and the effect is strongest for the underdog rung.
interactions.how_to_test: Bin games by expected total at constant expected gap and compare realised P(margin>=3) with the Skellam/negative-binomial prediction; check calibration of the 2.5 rung in low-total versus high-total bins.

interactions.hypothesis: A rest disadvantage matters mainly if the tired team starts its backup; when the starter plays anyway the residual penalty is small, so the rest flag should be conditioned on confirmed starter.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate the back-to-back coefficient separately for games with starter vs backup in net.

interactions.hypothesis: Weight on current-season xG rises with games played and saturates once a few dozen games are in; before that the posterior is dominated by the prior so large xG gaps early in the year should be discounted.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit blend weight against games played and test log-loss improvement versus a constant weight in October-November games.

interactions.hypothesis: Dormant in November: only after roughly game 70 do clinched or eliminated teams rest stars, and then a healthy scratch is persistent news only if rest is not strategic, so stakes decide whether an absence is a one-night event; before that window this interaction should be set to zero.
interactions.how_to_test: Restrict to games 72-82; compare star participation and goal-difference residuals for clinched/eliminated teams against all other games; in earlier months confirm the term adds nothing.

nonlinearities.shape: Concave in shots faced; heavily shrunk
nonlinearities.why: The information in goals-saved-above-expected grows with shots faced but with diminishing returns, and early-season GSAx has near-zero predictive weight so the effective coefficient is a concave function of sample size.

nonlinearities.shape: Step in lead size and time remaining
nonlinearities.why: Empty-net goal probability is near zero except for one-goal leads inside the last few minutes, then jumps; models that average over game time understate the 2.5 rung.

nonlinearities.shape: Tails fatten with expected total
nonlinearities.why: Higher total environments widen the goal-difference distribution, so the same expected gap implies higher probability of a three-goal margin; spread rung probabilities are convex in total.

mechanism_review.summary: Win and margin contracts are functionals of the final goal-difference distribution. Each team's regulation goals are an overdispersed count with mean set by shot volume, shot quality and the opposing goalie; the difference has a near-symmetric bell shape centred on the rating gap plus home ice. The winner contract then adds a resolution rule for regulation ties: overtime and a shootout decide the point with something close to a coin flip, so full-game win probability is a compressed version of regulation win probability. Spread rungs of 1.5 and 2.5 are tail masses of the same distribution, shaped by empty-net goals that convert one-goal leads into two-goal margins and by score effects that make leaders defend. Information arrives mostly as goalie and lineup confirmations in the hours before puck drop, so the main source of mispricing is the speed and size of translating lineup news into expected goal difference, not the base rating.

stages.name: Team strength to expected goal difference
stages.description: Each team's rating is built from score-adjusted 5v5 xG share, special-teams xG and goaltending, then combined into an expected regulation goal difference for this pairing with a home-ice constant. Early in the season (now is early November, roughly a dozen games in) current-season xG is a noisy estimate and must be blended with a preseason prior built from last year's rating, roster turnover and age; the blend weight on current data grows with games played. Opponent adjustment and score-effects correction matter because leading teams are outshot.
stages.distribution: Latent team ratings with posterior uncertainty (sd of order 0.15-0.25 goals per game early in the year); realised goal difference per game has sd near 2.3 goals.

stages.name: Goalie and lineup confirmation shocks
stages.description: Starting goalies are confirmed 1-3 hours before puck drop; replacing a strong starter with a backup moves the opponent's expected goals by a few tenths per game, and a missing top skater or defence pair moves the team's own rate. The size of the shock depends on who the replacement is and on how many minutes shift, so status alone (out/in) is not enough; a value-over-replacement estimate per player turns news into a goal-difference delta. Second games of back-to-backs raise backup probability and add travel fatigue.
stages.distribution: Discrete scenario mixture (starter A or B per team) with continuous skater-impact adjustment; confirmation timing is stochastic and information-vintage sensitive.

stages.name: Margin shaping: score effects and empty-net goals
stages.description: Final margin is not the 60-minute margin of a stationary process: teams with the lead shoot less, and after the trailing goalie is pulled empty-net goals add to the leader's margin. A one-goal lead at 3:00 left converts to a margin of two or more with large probability, so tails at 1.5 and 2.5 are fatter than a pure Skellam of full-game rates implies. The pull time and 6v5 success rate differ by team and coach. Pregame, score_state rates are integrated over a ratings-only script distribution, never over a market-implied win probability or total.
stages.distribution: Skellam core with a late-game jump component; empty-net goals add +1 to the leader's margin with a conversion probability that is NOT yet estimated from data (see ml7) when a one-goal lead holds past 3:00.

stages.name: Regulation ties, overtime and shootout resolution
stages.description: About a quarter of regular-season games are level after 60 minutes; the winner contract then depends on a five-minute 3v3 period and a shootout. 3v3 overtime is high-event and star-driven, and shootout is near a coin flip with small shooter and goalie effects, so conditional on a tie the win probability sits within a few points of 50 percent with a small home edge. The settlement mapping also matters: a decided shootout is a one-goal margin and goals scored in OT count as ordinary goals for margin. KXNHLGAME and KXNHLSPREAD also list playoff games, where a regulation tie goes to 20-minute 5v5 sudden-death periods with no shootout, so the tie-resolution step must switch to the playoff OT hazard (still a +/-1 margin atom).
stages.distribution: Bernoulli resolution with p near 0.5 conditional on tie (a few points of rating-driven tilt); overtime adds a one-goal-margin atom, never two or more.

pace_volume.note: Pace and expected total set the variance of the goal difference and therefore the 1.5 and 2.5 rung tails; carried by total_goal_dispersion (expected total, dispersion) rather than a separate pace input.

officiating_rules.note: Referee crews shift penalty counts for both teams symmetrically and their effect on the goal difference is second-order relative to goalie and lineup swings; the OT format rule is handled under settlement.

required_data.timestamp_requirement: Only games finished before the as-of date; data vendor revisions to xG models must be vintaged.
required_data.history_needed: 2012-13 onward for xG (location data), 2007-08 for attempts.

candidate_sources.note: team and game CSVs with xG
